To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
resting state glutamate predicts pre-stimulus EEG alpha and that pre-stimulus activity predicts self-referential perception.
pre-stimulus EEG alpha power predicts the self-relatedness of subsequent stimuli and is related to glutamate levels in the PACC, a brain region that is associated with self-relatedness.

resting state glutamate in the perigenual ACC predicts elevated alpha power prior to the presentation of a self-relevant stimulus, and that this elevated alpha power predicts a high degree of self-relatedness of the stimulus.

the neurotemporal and neurobiochemical mechanisms that underpin the “rest-self”-overlap.
the neurotemporal and neurochemical mechanisms of the rest-self overlap.
the neurotemporal and neurochemical mechanisms of the rest-self overlap in anterior midline structures.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the pre-stimulus power of alpha oscillations in anterior cortical mid-line structures, which are known to be involved in self-referential processes, are related to the degree of self-relatedness of a stimulus and are mediated by resting glutamate concentration in these structures.

our results show pre-stimulus power of the alpha rhythm and resting state glutamatergic neurotransmission to mediate restself overlap that disposes or inclines subjects to assign high self-relatedness to perceived stimuli.
the pre-stimulus EEG alpha power and the resting glutamate level in PACC are the neurochemical and neurotemporal markers for self-relatedness.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
pre-stimulus activity and resting state glutamatergic neurotransmission may mediate rest-self overlaps that dispose or incline us to assign self-relatedness to stimuli.
glutamate in the PACC is associated with the degree to which subjects’ perception of stimuli is self-related.
pre-stimulus EEG power and resting state metabolites in the PACC can be used to predict subjects’ self-referential perception and judgment.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the neural overlap between resting and self-referencing activity is reflected in the temporal and spectral domain.
the neural mechanisms that underpin self-relatedness can be identified by combining neurophysiological (EEG) and neurobiochemical (MRS) techniques.
pre-stimulus power changes in alpha and glutamate concentration in the PACC are predictive for the degree to which subjects assign stimuli to be self-related.
